title: The Toll Paid Back
endLine: A potassium channel selects by repaying the toll, not by size.

scenes.tts: The first film showed a channel lowering the toll for leaving water. A potassium channel goes further. It passes potassium more than a thousand times more readily than sodium. Yet sodium is the smaller ion. How can a pore turn away the smaller ion?
scenes.narration: The first film showed a channel lowering the toll for leaving water. A potassium channel goes further. It passes K⁺ more than a thousand times more readily than Na⁺. Yet Na⁺ is the smaller ion. How can a pore turn away the smaller ion?
scenes.caption: The first film showed a channel lowering the toll for leaving water. A potassium channel goes further. It passes K⁺ more than a thousand times more readily than Na⁺. Yet Na⁺ is the smaller ion. How can a pore turn away the smaller ion?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's world and colour map without a reset: one horizontal schematic bilayer, BLUE water above and below (sides left unlabelled in this film, since flow follows the gradient) with drifting BLUE water motes, a broad GOLD oily core, and the TEAL channel from the first film spanning the core with its BLUE grip dots. COLOUR BY CONCEPT, kept all film: water and water-shell droplets BLUE; oily core GOLD; channel walls TEAL; the oxygens lining the filter are the same BLUE grip dots (drawn as plain dots, no molecular structure); sodium YELLOW circles with a plus sign, as in the first film; potassium VIOLET circles with a plus sign, drawn slightly larger than sodium; the toll for leaving water RED, as the first film's toll bar; energy paid back TEAL. A small 'schematic' tag sits at bottom right throughout. The membrane fills about 65% of the frame height with the teal channel at centre. During the first sentence, a YELLOW sodium circle wearing its six BLUE water droplets reaches the channel; the droplets hand off to the grip dots and it passes, while the first film's RED toll bar at left shrinks (a recap of the first film). On 'potassium channel', the teal channel narrows into a tall tube labelled 'potassium channel'. VIOLET potassium circles stream down through it one after another; a smaller YELLOW sodium circle approaches the top, bumps the entrance and bounces back into the upper water, twice. A counter beside the tube ticks 'potassium: 1000' against 'sodium: 1' as ions pass (ratio from the lesson, 'more than a thousand times'). On 'smaller ion', the two circles are set side by side above the tube with a short bracket showing the yellow one is smaller. White question text across the top: 'Why is the smaller ion refused?' Water motes keep drifting.

Title 'The Toll Paid Back' fades in above the tube for two seconds while the question text fades out. VIOLET potassium circles keep streaming down the tube; the YELLOW sodium circle drifts in the upper water. Water motes keep moving.

scenes.tts: Look at the narrowest stretch of the pore, the selectivity filter. It is a short tube lined mostly with oxygens. Four binding sites sit in a row. Each site is a cage of eight oxygens. A sieve this narrow would favour sodium.
scenes.narration: Look at the narrowest stretch of the pore, the selectivity filter. It is a short tube lined mostly with oxygens. Four binding sites sit in a row. Each site is a cage of eight oxygens. A sieve this narrow would favour Na⁺.
scenes.caption: Look at the narrowest stretch of the pore, the selectivity filter. It is a short tube lined mostly with oxygens. Four binding sites sit in a row. Each site is a cage of eight oxygens. A sieve this narrow would favour Na⁺.
scenes.visual: Camera dives into the narrowest part of the teal tube until it fills about 70% of the frame height; the bilayer stays visible as GOLD bands at left and right. Label 'selectivity filter'. On 'lined mostly with oxygens', BLUE grip dots light up along both inner walls. On 'four binding sites', the dots gather into four stacked rings, top to bottom, labelled 'S1' to 'S4'. On 'cage of eight oxygens', one ring rotates slowly to show its eight BLUE dots, tagged '8 oxygens'. On 'a sieve', a grey sieve outline briefly overlays the tube and a ghost YELLOW circle slips through it, then the sieve outline fades with a small question mark.

scenes.tts: To enter, potassium must shed its water shell and pay the toll. Inside a site, eight oxygens sit close, where its water sat. They pay back nearly all of it. So potassium enters at little net cost.
scenes.narration: To enter, K⁺ must shed its water shell and pay the toll. Inside a site, eight oxygens sit close, where its water sat. They pay back nearly all of it. So K⁺ enters at little net cost.
scenes.caption: To enter, K⁺ must shed its water shell and pay the toll. Inside a site, eight oxygens sit close, where its water sat. They pay back nearly all of it. So K⁺ enters at little net cost.
scenes.visual: A VIOLET potassium circle wearing six BLUE water droplets descends to the top of the filter. Beside the tube, a vertical energy bar (schematic) is carried in. On 'shed its water shell', the droplets peel away and the RED toll bar rises. On 'eight oxygens sit close', the eight BLUE dots of the top site close in until they touch the violet circle all round. On 'pay back', a TEAL bar fills downward against the RED bar until only a thin red sliver is left, labelled 'small net cost'. The violet ion settles into the site, gently jiggling.

scenes.tts: Sodium holds its water shell more tightly, so its toll is larger. In the classic snug-fit picture, sodium is too small to touch all eight oxygens at once. It sheds its water but is not paid back enough. So it stalls.
scenes.narration: Na⁺ holds its water shell more tightly, so its toll is larger. In the classic snug-fit picture, Na⁺ is too small to touch all eight oxygens at once. It sheds its water but is not paid back enough. So it stalls.
scenes.caption: Na⁺ holds its water shell more tightly, so its toll is larger. In the classic snug-fit picture, Na⁺ is too small to touch all eight oxygens at once. It sheds its water but is not paid back enough. So it stalls.
scenes.visual: Same filter and bar. A YELLOW sodium circle with its BLUE droplets, held visibly closer than potassium's, comes to the top site. On 'toll is larger', the droplets peel away and a taller RED bar rises beside the first one. On 'too small to touch', the eight BLUE dots stay in their ring; the small yellow circle rattles inside and touches only two or three at a time, each touch flashing. Tag 'snug-fit picture'. On 'not paid back enough', the TEAL payback bar fills only part way, leaving a tall red remainder. On 'stalls', the sodium circle backs out of the site and hovers at the entrance while a violet ion below continues down.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. The filter does not sort ions by size. It sorts them by how much of each toll it pays back.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. The filter does not sort ions by size. It sorts them by how much of each toll it pays back.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. The filter does not sort ions by size. It sorts them by how much of each toll it pays back.
scenes.visual: Pull back slightly so the filter, the two toll bars and both ions share the frame. On 'not by size', the size bracket from the hook reappears over the two circles, then fades. On 'how much of each toll', the two bar pairs slide next to each other: potassium's RED bar almost fully covered by TEAL, sodium's taller RED bar only partly covered. Labels under them: 'potassium: nearly repaid' and 'sodium: underpaid'. Violet ions keep stepping down through the four sites.

scenes.tts: How exact must that payback be? Sodium's toll is about seventy kilojoules per mole larger than potassium's. At body temperature, every six kilojoules buys about a tenfold preference. A thousandfold is three tenfolds: about eighteen.
scenes.narration: How exact must that payback be? Na⁺'s toll is about 70 kJ/mol larger than K⁺'s. At body temperature, every 6 kJ/mol buys about a tenfold preference. A thousandfold is three tenfolds: about 18.
scenes.caption: How exact must that payback be? Na⁺'s toll is about 70 kJ/mol larger than K⁺'s. At body temperature, every 6 kJ/mol buys about a tenfold preference. A thousandfold is three tenfolds: about 18.
scenes.visual: The two bar pairs transform into one computed bar chart in kilojoules per mole, axis 0 to 80, ticks every 10, label 'kJ per mole'. On 'seventy', a RED bar rises to 70, labelled 'extra toll: sodium'. On 'about eighteen', a narrow white bracket appears at the top of that bar spanning 18 (17.8 from the lesson: RT times ln 1000 at 37 °C), labelled 'needed for 1000 to 1'. The filter stays small at left with ions moving. On 'every six kilojoules', a WHITE note beside the chart reads '~5.9 kJ/mol per 10x at 37 °C'; on 'three tenfolds', it adds '10 x 10 x 10 = 1000; 3 x 5.9 ≈ 18'.

scenes.tts: So the filter could even pay sodium back more than potassium: seventy minus eighteen leaves fifty-two to spare. It would still favour potassium a thousandfold. Simulations suggest the oxygens do give sodium more. Just not enough more.
scenes.narration: So the filter could even pay Na⁺ back more than K⁺: 70 minus 18 leaves 52 to spare. It would still favour K⁺ a thousandfold. Simulations suggest the oxygens do give Na⁺ more. Just not enough more.
scenes.caption: So the filter could even pay Na⁺ back more than K⁺: 70 minus 18 leaves 52 to spare. It would still favour K⁺ a thousandfold. Simulations suggest the oxygens do give Na⁺ more. Just not enough more.
scenes.visual: On the same chart, a TEAL bar grows up inside the RED 70 bar from 0 to 52, labelled 'extra payback allowed'; the white 18 bracket stays on top, uncovered (70 minus 52 is 18). On 'simulations suggest', a TEAL ghost bar labelled 'simulations' rises inside the red bar to an unnumbered height below the 52 line (schematic), short of closing the gap. In the small filter at left, the yellow sodium ion still hovers at the entrance. On 'seventy minus eighteen', a WHITE line beside the chart reads '70 − 18 = 52'.

scenes.tts: But a site that repays potassium so well should hold on to it. Yet around a hundred million potassium ions can cross each second. What lets a tightly held ion leave?
scenes.narration: But a site that repays K⁺ so well should hold on to it. Yet around a hundred million K⁺ ions can cross each second. What lets a tightly held ion leave?
scenes.caption: But a site that repays K⁺ so well should hold on to it. Yet around a hundred million K⁺ ions can cross each second. What lets a tightly held ion leave?
scenes.visual: The chart fades; the filter grows back to fill about 70% of the frame. One VIOLET ion sits deep in a site, with the eight BLUE dots snug around it, and a small TEAL 'held' glow. On 'a hundred million', a counter beside the tube reads 'about 100,000,000 per second'. Question card at top in white: 'What lets it leave?'

Predict pause. The question card stays. The held violet ion jiggles in place inside its ring of eight blue dots; one more violet ion waits above the filter but does not enter. Water motes drift. No other change.

scenes.tts: The answer is probably crowding. Several potassium ions sit in the filter at once, and like charges repel. When another ion enters, that repulsion lowers the barrier for the leading ion to leave. This is the knock-on mechanism.
scenes.narration: The answer is probably crowding. Several K⁺ ions sit in the filter at once, and like charges repel. When another ion enters, that repulsion lowers the barrier for the leading ion to leave. This is the knock-on mechanism.
scenes.caption: The answer is probably crowding. Several K⁺ ions sit in the filter at once, and like charges repel. When another ion enters, that repulsion lowers the barrier for the leading ion to leave. This is the knock-on mechanism.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. Two more VIOLET ions are shown already sitting in other sites, so three sit in the four-site filter, each with a plus sign. On 'like charges repel', short red push arrows appear between neighbouring ions. On 'another ion enters', the waiting ion steps into the top site; the push arrows brighten, and the lowest ion lifts out of its site and drops into the lower water. The row shifts down one site. Repeat the cycle at a steady rhythm. Label 'knock-on'.

scenes.tts: A Newton's cradle is a fair image, but only an image. No collision passes energy along. Whether water molecules separate the ions is still argued, though recent evidence favours direct contact.
scenes.narration: A Newton's cradle is a fair image, but only an image. No collision passes energy along. Whether water molecules separate the ions is still argued, though recent evidence favours direct contact.
scenes.caption: A Newton's cradle is a fair image, but only an image. No collision passes energy along. Whether water molecules separate the ions is still argued, though recent evidence favours direct contact.
scenes.visual: Knock-on cycle keeps running. On 'Newton's cradle', a small cradle icon swings once at the side of the tube, then a white cross marks the swinging ball, tagged 'image only'. On 'water molecules separate', a BLUE water droplet flickers between two violet ions, with a tag 'still argued'; it fades to half brightness while the two ions touch directly, with a tag 'recent evidence: contact'. Neither picture is erased.

scenes.tts: So one short tube is both picky and fast. It hands potassium back almost its whole toll, and sodium too little. Crowding keeps potassium moving. Size never decided it. The payback did.
scenes.narration: So one short tube is both picky and fast. It hands K⁺ back almost its whole toll, and Na⁺ too little. Crowding keeps K⁺ moving. Size never decided it. The payback did.
scenes.caption: So one short tube is both picky and fast. It hands K⁺ back almost its whole toll, and Na⁺ too little. Crowding keeps K⁺ moving. Size never decided it. The payback did.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening composition: the carried bilayer, the tall teal potassium channel and blue water. VIOLET ions stream steadily down the tube in the knock-on rhythm. On 'almost its whole toll', a small RED-and-TEAL bar pair beside the tube shows red nearly covered; on 'sodium too little', a second pair shows red mostly uncovered while a YELLOW sodium circle bounces off the entrance. On 'size never decided it', the size bracket over the two circles fades out for good; on 'the payback did', both TEAL bars pulse.

End card over the dimmed but still moving channel world (violet potassium ions streaming down the tube, a yellow sodium circle drifting outside, water motes moving). Large white text, centred: 'A potassium channel selects by repaying the toll, not by size.'
